q: You are leaving a quay in a fresh crosswind. The stern line will be under load until the moment you let it go. Which knot do you tie to the ring?
a: Round turn and two half hitches
o: Bowline through the ring
Clove hitch and a half hitch
Figure of eight through the ring
why: The round turn takes the load, so the half hitches can be cast off and the line eased even while it is loaded.

fig.note: Leaving: you let go under load

q: You come alongside a fishing quay with bollards. Your crew steps ashore with the bow line and wants a fixed loop in its end to drop over a bollard. Which knot?
a: Bowline
o: Clove hitch
Rolling hitch
Reef knot
why: A bowline makes a fixed loop that will not slip or jam, and unties easily once the load is off.

q: Hours into a long starboard tack, the genoa sheet has a riding turn on the winch and will not ease. What do you do?
a: Take the load off with a rolling hitch led to another winch
o: Winch in harder until the jammed turns jump free
Lift the turns off the drum while it is still loaded
Take a clove hitch on the sheet to the nearest cleat
why: A rolling hitch grips a loaded line along its length; with the strain on another winch the riding turn can be cleared.

fig.note: Riding turn: the sheet is jammed on the drum

q: You are hanging fenders on the guardrail before entering a harbour where you will change their height at each berth. Which hitch do you use?
a: Clove hitch, with a half hitch on top
o: Bowline, tied round the rail
Reef knot, tied round the rail
Sheet bend, tied round the rail
why: A clove hitch is quick to tie and to adjust on a rail; the half hitch stops it working loose.

fig.note: Fender heights change at each berth

q: Your stern line is too short to reach the bollard, so you join a thinner spare line to it. Which knot?
a: A double sheet bend
o: A reef knot
A clove hitch
A figure of eight
why: A sheet bend joins lines of different thickness; doubled, it holds better in slippery synthetic rope.

q: Before a night passage your crew re-reeves the genoa sheets through the cars. What goes in the end of each sheet?
a: A figure-of-eight stopper knot
o: A bowline loop
A clove hitch round the car
A half hitch round the track
why: A figure of eight stops the sheet running out through the car and is easy to undo.

q: Your crew has made the loaded bow line fast: a turn round the base, a figure of eight, then three locking hitches piled on top. What do you tell them?
a: Take off two hitches — one locking hitch is enough
o: Leave it — each extra hitch adds holding
Add a bowline over the horn as well
Take off the turn round the base first
why: Turn, figure of eight, one locking hitch: more hitches can jam under load and slow you when you need to let go.

fig.note: Turn · figure of eight · 3 locking hitches

q: You are stowing the dinghy on deck for this passage. How do you lash it?
a: Several turns to strong points, frapped tight, finished with hitches
o: One line over the middle, tied off to the guardrail
Shock cord to the handrails, so it can give in a sea
Loose on deck, so it can be launched in a hurry
why: A lashing takes several turns to strong points and frapping turns tighten it; guardrails and shock cord give way in a sea.

fig.title: Before a 40-mile passage
lines: Dinghy upside down on the coachroof

q: After a swim your crew is exhausted in the water beside the boat and the ladder has broken. You will lift her with the main halyard. What do you tie in the middle of a spare line to make a sling?
a: A bowline on the bight
o: A clove hitch round her chest
A running bowline under her arms
A reef knot round her waist
why: A bowline on the bight gives two fixed loops in the middle of a line that will not tighten: a seat and a chest loop.

q: You are holding off the waiting pontoon and must get a line to the marinero. How do you throw it?
a: Make the end fast, split the coil, throw past him into the wind
o: Throw the whole coil in one bundle straight at him
Make the end fast, throw short and let the wind carry it
Tie a fender to the end to give it weight, then throw
why: Secure the standing end and throw the outer half of a split coil overarm; aim beyond him, as the wind will check it.

fig.note: Marinero on the pontoon, 10 m to port, upwind

q: You have bought a new length of three-strand nylon to make a mooring line with a permanent eye. How do you finish it?
a: An eye splice at one end, a whipping on the other
o: A bowline at one end, a stopper knot on the other
An eye splice at one end, an overhand knot on the other
A figure-of-eight loop at one end, nothing on the other
why: A splice keeps most of the rope's strength and never shakes loose; a whipping stops the cut end unlaying.

q: You are choosing rope for each item on this list. Which choice is right?
a: Nylon for the warp and mooring lines, low-stretch for the halyard
o: Low-stretch for the warp and mooring lines, nylon for the halyard
Polypropylene for all three — it floats and costs less
The same polyester braid for all three items
why: Nylon stretches to absorb snatching at anchor and in a berth; a halyard must not stretch or the sail loses its shape.

q: You arrive in this Breton anchorage two hours after high water to stay the night. Where do you anchor?
a: B — sand, and enough water at LW
o: A — sand, and the closest in to shelter
C — the weed holds well among the moorings
A — 4.2 m is plenty for a 1.9 m draft
why: Depth at LW = depth now − 3.0 m: A 1.2 m (aground), B 4.5 m; C is weed among moorings — poor holding, no room.

fig.note: Depths now · 3.0 m still to fall to LW · draft 1.9 m

q: You are anchored off the east coast of an island in an offshore westerly. What do you do about tonight's forecast?
a: Move before dark to a bay sheltered from the north-east
o: Stay, and let out more chain as the wind veers
Stay — a NE wind blows along this coast, not onto it
Move at midnight, when the wind starts to veer
why: Veering W → N → NE turns this east coast into a lee shore at night; move in daylight to shelter from the NE.

fig.note: Forecast: W 4, veering N, then NE 5 after midnight

q: You are motoring to your chosen spot to anchor. How do you make the approach?
a: Slowly into the wind, stop, let go as she starts to go astern
o: Downwind with way on, let go and let her swing round
Slowly into the wind, let go while still going ahead
Across the wind, let go and let all the chain run
why: Head to wind gives control; letting go as she moves astern lays the chain out in a line, not in a heap on the anchor.

fig.note: Final approach to the spot, 6 m of water

q: You anchor at low water in a Breton river to stay for 24 hours. What is the least chain you let out?
a: About 32 m
o: About 18 m
About 28 m
About 14 m
why: Work from the HW depth at the bow: (3.6 + 3.4 + 1.0) × 4 = 32 m.

q: You anchor at high water on this rode for a settled night. What is the least you let out?
a: About 54 m — 6:1 for a mostly rope rode
o: About 36 m — 4:1, as for all chain
About 32 m — 4:1 of the water depth
About 27 m — 3:1 is plenty in F3
why: A rope rode needs more scope than chain, about 6:1 or more: (8 + 1) × 6 = 54 m.

q: You have let out 30 m of chain. How do you check that the anchor is holding?
a: Go astern to firm revs and watch the transit abeam
o: Watch the chain: taut means the anchor is holding
Watch the depth: if it stays the same, she holds
Wait for her to lie head to wind, then go below
why: Back down under power to set it; a transit abeam that stays closed shows the boat is not moving over the ground.

fig.note: Anchor down, 30 m out · chapel and rock in line abeam

q: You set the plotter's anchor alarm for the night. Where do you centre it, and how big do you make it?
a: On the anchor, radius about 42 m
o: On the boat now, radius about 42 m
On the anchor, radius about 15 m
On the boat now, radius about 100 m
why: She swings round the anchor: √(30² − 6²) ≈ 29 m of chain + 12 m of boat ≈ 42 m; centred on the boat it alarms on a swing.

fig.title: Setting the anchor alarm
lines: Depth 5 m, bow roller 1 m above water
Anchor position marked on the plotter

q: Your anchor is down and holding. Will you swing clear of the rock tonight?
a: No — her stern can reach about 46 m from the anchor
o: Yes — she cannot go more than 35 m from the anchor
Yes — she stays within the chain's run, about 34 m
Yes — on all chain she barely swings, about 12 m
why: Swing radius ≈ the chain's horizontal run plus the boat: √(35² − 6²) ≈ 34 m + 12 m ≈ 46 m — past the rock at 40 m.

fig.title: Swinging room
lines: 35 m chain out, depth 5 m, roller 1 m
Rock awash 40 m east of your anchor

q: You decide to stay the night here. How do you run it?
a: Anchor watches in turns, engine ready, alarm on
o: All turn in; the plotter's alarm will wake you
You stay up alone all night so the crew can sleep
Let out all the chain, then everyone turns in
why: In rising wind someone must be awake on deck: a rota of anchor watches, with the engine and a plan ready.

q: You are on deck in seconds. What do you do?
a: Start the engine, motor up to ease the load, re-anchor
o: Let all the remaining chain run out at once
Drop the kedge over the stern to stop her
Wait — a dragging anchor usually resets itself
why: Engine first, to take the strain and keep control; then lift and re-anchor with more scope, or move.

fig.title: 0230 at anchor
lines: The transit has opened: you are moving

q: You must anchor overnight in this narrow tidal river with little swinging room. How?
a: A Bahamian moor: anchors up and downstream, the bow between
o: Two anchors in tandem on one chain, both upstream
One anchor with extra scope to ride the turn of tide
Bow and stern anchors, so she lies across the stream
why: A Bahamian moor holds the bow between two anchors laid up and down the stream, so she turns in little more than her length.

fig.note: River 80 m wide · the stream turns every 6 h

q: You have run onto a sandbank at the mouth of a river. How do you get off?
a: Lay the kedge astern into deep water by dinghy and haul on it
o: Go full astern now until she slides off the sand
Wait aboard: the rising tide will float her off as she is
Let go the bower anchor at the bow and wait for the tide
why: A kedge laid in deep water holds her against the wind as the tide rises and lets you haul her off; hard astern sucks up sand.

q: You decide to anchor here for the night. What do you rig?
a: A tripping line from the anchor's crown to a small buoy
o: Extra scope, so the anchor digs in deeper
A second anchor on the same chain
A rope rode, so it is cheaper to cut away
why: A tripping line pulls the anchor out backwards by its crown if it hooks under old chain or rock.

fig.title: Pilot book: the anchorage
lines: Good shelter from N and W

q: You are leaving this crowded bay. How do you weigh anchor?
a: Motor gently up the chain as the bow crew points; the windlass only lifts
o: Let the windlass haul the boat up to the anchor
Break it out at full ahead, then lift it on the move
Lift it with the engine off, so the propeller is safe
why: Motor up to the anchor so the windlass only lifts the chain; the crew's hand signals show where it lies and when it breaks out.

fig.note: Y = you · 1–3 yachts at anchor, 30–40 m off

q: You will go stern-to this quay on your own anchor, with the wind across the harbour. Where do you let go?
a: About 45 m out, a little upwind of your slot
o: About 30 m out, a little upwind of your slot
About 45 m out, a little downwind of your slot
About 15 m out, straight off your slot
why: (7 + 1) × 4 = 32 m of chain plus 12 m of boat ≈ 45 m; let go upwind, as the wind pushes you down while you reverse.

fig.note: Depth 7 m · roller 1 m · 4:1 · boat 12 m

q: You put the engine astern from rest on a calm day. What does the stern do first?
a: Kicks to port
o: Kicks to starboard
Goes straight back
Stays put; the bow swings to port
why: A right-handed propeller walks the stern to port going astern, most strongly before she gathers way.

fig.note: Going astern from rest · right-handed propeller

q: You can choose which side to put to this pontoon. Which, and why?
a: Port side to — going astern to stop pulls the stern in
o: Starboard side to — going astern pulls the stern in
Port side to — going astern swings the bow in
Either side — prop walk only acts at speed
why: Astern kicks the stern to port, so port side to, the brake also brings the stern in alongside.

fig.title: Visitors' pontoon
lines: Space on either side of the hammerhead

q: You must turn round in this marina fairway. Which way do you turn?
a: To starboard: ahead with full helm, then astern, and repeat
o: To port: prop walk astern swings the bow to port
To port: ahead and astern with the helm hard to port
Either way: prop walk cancels out over a turn
why: Astern kicks the stern to port and the bow to starboard: it helps a clockwise turn and fights an anticlockwise one.
ref: Boat handling — turning in a tight space

fig.note: Fairway two boat lengths wide · right-handed prop

q: You motor ahead off this quay and put the helm hard to port to turn away. What does the stern do?
a: Swings to starboard, towards the quay
o: Swings to port, away from the quay
Follows the bow straight out
Stays where it is while the bow turns
why: Going ahead she pivots about a third of her length from the bow, so the stern swings opposite the turn — into the quay.

fig.note: Starboard side to, leaving ahead

q: You are coming alongside the waiting pontoon in this river. Which way do you head for the final approach?
a: East, into the stream, as the moored yachts lie
o: West, into the wind — a yacht always lies to it
West, with the stream, to keep steerage way
North, straight in, so neither has a grip
why: Approach into whichever acts more on the boat — here the 2 kn stream, as the moored yachts show by lying head to it.

fig.note: Mooring buoys in yellow

q: You want to drop into this gap on the pontoon to starboard against a 2 kn stream. How?
a: Stem the stream at its speed, angle the bow slightly in, crab across
o: Run down with the stream and go hard astern at the gap
Stem the stream at its speed, angle the bow slightly out
Turn in at 90°, bow first, and let the stream swing her
why: Ferry gliding: stemming the stream at its speed holds you still; a small angle of the bow towards the berth moves you sideways.

fig.note: Gap: one boat length + 4 m

q: You are pinned starboard side to by the wind, with boats close ahead and astern. How do you get off?
a: Bow line led aft, fender the bow, slow ahead; stern out, then astern
o: Stern line led forward, slow astern; bow out, then ahead
Push the bow off hard, then motor ahead with helm to port
Let go everything and go full astern with helm to port
why: Ahead on a bow spring swings the stern out into the wind; then astern, and prop walk to port carries the stern further off.

fig.note: Wind F5 onto the pontoon · right-handed prop

q: The wind is blowing you off this pontoon. Your crew has made a midships line, led aft, fast to a pontoon cleat. What now?
a: Slow ahead, wheel turned away from the pontoon
o: Slow ahead, wheel turned towards the pontoon
Slow astern, wheel turned away from the pontoon
Neutral, and the crew hauls her in by hand
why: Ahead against a midships spring pulls her in bodily; the wheel turned away from the pontoon stops the stern swinging out.

fig.note: Wind F4 off the pontoon · midships spring on

q: You are picking up this mooring buoy under power. How do you make the final approach?
a: Heading west, into the stream, slowly
o: Heading east, with the stream, slowly
Heading north, across the stream, then stop
Heading east, then astern to stop beside it
why: Stem the stream: you keep steerage at low speed and can stop over the ground with the buoy at the bow.

q: The marinero hands the lazy line up to you at the stern. What do you do with it?
a: Walk it to the bow outside everything, haul it taut, cleat it
o: Cleat it at the stern next to the stern line
Let it drop: the two stern lines hold you in place
Walk it forward inside the shrouds, cleat it slack
why: The lazy line holds the bow off the quay: take it forward clear of everything, haul taut, cleat at the bow; keep it out of the prop.

fig.title: Stern-to, Croatian marina
lines: Stern lines on, engine slow ahead
Marinero hands you the lazy line
Its sinker is well ahead of the bow

q: The town quay is full and you are told to raft outside a larger yacht. How do you lie?
a: Lines to her and your own shore lines; masts staggered
o: Lines to her only; she holds both boats on hers
Lines to her and shore lines; masts level abeam
Shore lines only, with fenders against her side
why: Your own shore lines take your weight off her; masts staggered so the spreaders cannot lock as you roll.

q: You will sail onto this mooring buoy. With which sail do you make the final approach?
a: Jib only — furl it to slow down as you stem the tide
o: Main only — luff head to wind to stop at the buoy
Main only — ease the sheet to stop as you stem the tide
Full sail — luff head to wind beside the buoy
why: You stem the tide, so the wind is astern: a mainsail cannot be spilled downwind, a jib can be furled or let fly.

fig.note: Approaching the buoy under sail

q: You will sail off the anchor here. The main is up and the chain is up and down. How do you get her heading east, on port tack, as the anchor breaks out?
a: Back the jib to port, so the bow pays off to starboard
o: Back the jib to starboard, so the bow pays off to starboard
Back the jib to starboard, so the bow pays off to port
Sheet the main hard in, so the bow pays off to starboard
why: A jib held aback on the port side pushes the bow to starboard: port tack, heading east, away from the rocks.

fig.note: Wind N 3 · open water to the east

q: You want to heave to so the crew can reef in peace. How?
a: Tack, leave the jib sheet made fast, ease the main, tiller to leeward
o: Tack, leave the jib sheet made fast, sheet the main in, tiller to windward
Gybe, leave the jib sheet made fast, ease the main, tiller amidships
Luff head to wind, drop the jib, lash the tiller amidships
why: Hove to, the backed jib pushes the bow off and the tiller lashed to leeward brings it up: she lies quietly, drifting slowly.

fig.note: Close-hauled, starboard tack · tiller steering

q: You put in the first reef. In what order?
a: Ease kicker and sheet, lower the halyard, fix the tack, re-hoist, pull the reef line
o: Pull the reef line first, then lower the halyard and fix the tack
Lower the halyard with the kicker still on, then fix the tack
Fix the tack, pull the reef line, then ease the kicker and sheet
why: Kicker and sheet off so the boom can rise; tack cringle on, halyard tight again, then the reef line pulls the clew down.

fig.title: Reefing at sea, F6
lines: Kicker and mainsheet still hard on

q: You are fighting the helm on this beat; the rudder is well over all the time. What do you do first?
a: Ease the traveller down and reef the main
o: Reef the genoa and leave the main as it is
Sheet the main harder to flatten it
Move the crew to leeward to steady her
why: Weather helm comes from too much main and heel: ease the traveller and reef the main, and the balance moves forward.

fig.note: Close-hauled F5 · heeled 30° · heavy weather helm

q: You will run like this for three hours before you gybe. How do you rig a preventer?
a: From the boom end, forward to a bow block, back to the cockpit
o: From the middle of the boom to the base of a shroud
From the boom end straight down to the toe rail abeam
No preventer: ease the kicker right off instead
why: Led from the boom end to the bow and aft, it holds the boom against a gybe and can be eased from the cockpit; mid-boom it can break.

fig.note: Running in F5 and a rolling sea

q: Your boat slams and stops on every third wave on this beat. How do you steer?
a: Bear away a little for speed; luff up the face, bear off over the top
o: Pinch as close to the wind as she will go
Bear away onto a beam reach and sail across the waves
Hold a dead straight course and let her punch through
why: Steering a little free keeps her moving; luff into the face, bear away over the crest so she does not fall off the top.

fig.note: Beating into a short, steep sea · F5

q: You are entering your berth in this marina in a fresh crosswind. What is the plan?
a: With way on, aim at the windward finger; first line: windward midships
o: Dead slow, aim at the middle; first line: leeward bow
With way on, aim at the leeward yacht; first line: windward stern
Dead slow, aim at the windward finger; first line: leeward stern
why: Some speed keeps steerage against the wind; aim upwind in the slot and get the windward midships line on first to stop her blowing down.

fig.note: Fingers in grey · fairway to the east

q: You have lost your engine and this yacht will tow you into port. How do you make her towline fast on your boat?
a: A bridle to both bow cleats, led through the bow roller
o: To one bow cleat, with a hitch you can slip
To the windlass drum, which is built for the load
To the pulpit, so it is clear of the stem
why: A bridle shares the load between strong points and keeps the line central; the windlass and pulpit are not built to tow.

fig.note: Engine failed · a yacht takes you in tow

q: You are towing this yacht. How long a towline, and how fast?
a: About 40 m, well below her hull speed
o: About 30 m, well below her hull speed
About 40 m, at about her hull speed
About 10 m, at about her hull speed
why: A multiple of the wave length (2 × 20 m) keeps both boats on the same part of a wave; near hull speed everything is overloaded.

q: You must turn your catamaran to port on the spot in this fairway. How?
a: Port engine astern, starboard engine ahead
o: Port engine ahead, starboard engine astern
Both engines ahead, rudders hard to port
Port engine astern only, rudders hard to port
why: The engines are far apart: one ahead and one astern spin her about her middle; port astern and starboard ahead turn her to port.

fig.note: Twin-engine catamaran · fairway 1.5 lengths wide

q: Your crew want to go back to the boat in one trip. What do you do?
a: Two trips, lifejackets on, kill cord on, torch showing
o: One trip, everyone sitting low and still
One trip, with the strongest swimmer outside
Two trips; lifejackets only for non-swimmers
why: Never overload; lifejackets, the kill cord and a light — an offshore wind carries a swamped dinghy out to sea.

fig.title: Taverna, 2300
lines: Five crew, dinghy rated for four
400 m to the boat, wind offshore F4
Outboard with kill cord, one torch

q: You are anchored for the night on all chain and want a nylon snubber to take the load off the windlass. There is no chain hook aboard. How do you fix the snubber to the chain?
a: A rolling hitch round the chain
o: A clove hitch round the chain
A sheet bend through a chain link
A reef knot round the chain
why: A rolling hitch grips along a loaded chain or line and will not slide; the snubber's stretch then takes the snatch off the windlass.

q: You are looking over this winch before a long passage. What do you do about it?
a: Re-lead the sheet so it meets the drum slightly from below
o: Put one more turn on the drum before it is loaded
Take a turn off the drum so the sheet runs freer
Tighten the self-tailer jaws so the turns stay down
why: A sheet must reach the drum a few degrees from below, so each turn is pushed up and clear; led down onto the drum, the turns ride over each other.

fig.title: Port genoa winch
lines: Four turns on the drum, self-tailer fine
New lead block: sheet runs down onto the drum

q: Your crew is about to open the clutch on the loaded main halyard to lower the sail for a reef. What do you tell her first?
a: Three turns on the winch, take the load, then open the clutch
o: Open the clutch, then quickly take turns on the winch
Open the clutch slowly, holding the tail in both hands
Put the handle in the winch, then open the clutch
why: A loaded clutch opened with no turns on the winch lets the halyard run and burns hands; take the load on the winch, then ease it out.

fig.note: Halyard held in a clutch, the sail fully loaded

q: Your crew must ease the loaded genoa sheet a few centimetres on a winch with no self-tailer. She has wrapped the tail twice round her hand for grip. What do you tell her?
a: Unwrap it; palm flat on the turns, ease a little at a time
o: Fine — the wraps give her the grip she needs
Flick all the turns off the drum, then re-wrap
Turn the winch handle backwards to ease it out
why: A loaded sheet can run without warning and drag a wrapped hand into the winch; ease with the palm on the turns and the tail free.

fig.note: No self-tailer · easing a few centimetres

q: You are buying a new painter for the dinghy you tow astern between anchorages. Which rope do you choose?
a: Floating polypropylene, so it stays clear of the propeller
o: Nylon, so it stretches when the dinghy snatches
Low-stretch polyester braid, so it stays short
Dyneema, so it is thin and very strong
why: A painter that sinks can wrap round the propeller when you go astern; floating polypropylene stays on the surface.

q: You are staying two nights on this quay. What do you do about your lines?
a: Chafe guards at the edge, double the lines, add snubbers
o: Haul every line bar-tight so she cannot move
Change to low-stretch lines, which wear less
Leave them; nylon is strong enough on its own
why: In a surge keep the stretch and stop the chafe: guards where the lines touch, doubled lines, and snubbers to soften each snatch.

fig.title: Harbour wall, swell running in
lines: Boat surging on her lines all night
Lines run over a rough concrete edge
Single nylon bow, stern and springs

q: You are coiling the long braided tail of the main halyard after hoisting, and every round turn twists it into kinks. How do you coil it?
a: In figure-of-eights, which add no twist
o: In clockwise turns, twisting each one in
In anticlockwise turns, twisting each one out
In tight turns round your hand and elbow
why: Braid has no lay, so round turns twist it; figure-of-eight loops cancel the twist and the line runs out clean.

q: You decide to lay the kedge in tandem with the bower. How is it rigged?
a: Kedge ahead of the bower, its chain shackled to the bower's crown
o: Kedge shackled to the bower's ring, the two side by side
Kedge on its own rode, dropped 30 m off to one side
Kedge slid halfway down the bower's chain as a weight
why: In tandem the kedge lies ahead on a short chain from the bower's crown, both in one line: for a strong wind from one steady direction.

fig.title: Gale tonight, open bay
lines: Weed over sand, holding only fair
Bower 20 kg; kedge 12 kg with 5 m chain

q: Your anchor is just below the surface, with the other chain hooked over it. How do you free it?
a: Pass a line under his chain, make it fast aboard, lower yours clear
o: Motor hard ahead to drag your anchor out from under it
Lift both higher on the windlass, then drop them with a jerk
Lower yours to the bottom again and motor away fast
why: Take his chain's weight on a line from your deck, lower your anchor clear of it, then slip the line from aboard.

fig.title: Leaving the town quay, Hydra
lines: You lay stern-to on your own anchor
It comes up with a chain across it
The neighbour's chain, laid over yours

q: You are leaving at dawn and the anchor will not break out. What do you do next?
a: Cleat the chain short, motor slowly the opposite way to the set
o: Keep the windlass hauling until the anchor breaks out
Cleat the chain short and go full ahead into the wind
Cut the chain at once and buoy the end to come back
why: Take the strain off the windlass, then pull from the other side: an anchor hooked under something often comes out the way it went in.

q: The anchor has started to drag again. What do you do?
a: Weigh and motor out to open water until daylight
o: Re-anchor closer in, where the water is shallower
Let out all the chain and set the alarm again
Re-anchor and hold her up on the engine all night
why: Holding has failed twice, the onshore wind is rising and rocks are close astern: sea room is the safe place until daylight.

fig.title: 0300 at anchor
lines: Rocks 150 m astern, open sea 1 M out
Engine fine, crew of four awake

q: You will anchor in this Greek bay before a blow. Which spot do you choose?
a: B — 7 m of sand: 40 m is 5:1 with the roller
o: A — 6 m of weed: it leaves the most chain spare
C — 9 m of sand: 40 m is over 4:1 of the depth
C — 9 m of sand: the bower holds best when deep
why: Scope counts from the bow roller: (7 + 1) × 5 = 40 m. At C you would need 50 m, and A's weed holds badly.

fig.note: No tide · 40 m chain, roller 1 m · 5:1 for F6

q: You are on all chain and arrive in this crowded bay for the night. Where do you anchor?
a: A — among the boats lying to chain, as you do
o: B — the boats on rope lie quietly, well apart
C — boats on buoys barely swing, so room is easy
B — just upwind of them, where the bottom is clear
why: Boats on similar rodes swing alike; rope rodes range widely and buoys hardly at all, so a chain boat among them touches when the wind shifts.

fig.note: Light winds, shifting overnight

q: You are writing the orders for tonight's anchor watch. Which do you write?
a: Call me if a bearing shifts, the wind tops F5, or a boat drags near
o: Call me only if the plotter's anchor alarm goes off
Call me at the end of each watch with a report
If she drags, let out more chain, then call me
why: The watch must know exactly when to wake you: the bearings that show dragging, a wind limit, another boat moving — before it is urgent.

q: The wind wakes you and you come up to find this. What do you do first?
a: Engine on, fenders out, horn and a torch to wake her crew
o: Call the coastguard on channel 16 and wait for them
Go to the bow to fend her off by hand as she comes
Weigh anchor at once and leave the bay in the dark
why: Be ready to move or take the blow, and wake her crew with sound and light; hands between two hulls in F6 get crushed.

fig.title: 0100 at anchor
lines: A yacht 50 m upwind is dragging onto you
No one moving on her deck
Wind F6; your anchor holding well

q: You are rigging a tripping line before you let go. How long do you make it?
a: About 8 m
o: About 4 m
About 6.5 m
About 13 m
why: Depth at HW 4.0 + 2.5 = 6.5 m; a little more keeps the buoy afloat at HW without a long loop on the surface at LW.

q: Your stern lines are on, but the bow is sagging downwind towards your neighbour. What do you do?
a: Tighten the anchor chain on the windlass, then trim the stern lines
o: Ease the anchor chain so the bow can settle by itself
Haul both stern lines bar-tight to pull her straight
Run a line from your bow to the neighbour's bow
why: The anchor holds the bow up to windward: take up the chain until she lies straight, then adjust the stern lines to keep clear of the quay.

fig.note: Stern lines on · your anchor 45 m out to the south

q: You anchor your catamaran for the night. How do you take the load off the windlass?
a: A bridle from both bows to a hook on the chain
o: Leave the chain on the windlass brake all night
A single snubber from one bow cleat to the chain
Make the chain fast round the foot of the mast
why: A bridle from both hulls holds the cat straight to the wind, takes the snatch off the windlass and stops her sheering about.

q: You anchor two hours after low water and will stay through high water. Using the rule of twelfths, what is the least chain you let out?
a: About 30 m
o: About 35 m
About 21 m
About 16 m

q: You engage astern from rest to back into your slot. What does the stern do first, and how do you allow for it?
a: Kicks to starboard: start with the stern a little to port of the line
o: Kicks to port: start with the stern a little to starboard of the line
Kicks to starboard: go astern dead slow all the way in
Goes straight back: prop walk only matters at speed
why: A left-handed propeller walks the stern to starboard going astern; aim off to port and get sternway on so the rudder takes over.

fig.title: Stern-to, calm harbour
lines: Your slot dead astern, 3 lengths off

q: Which way will her stern kick when you go astern from rest?
a: To starboard — she behaves like a left-handed prop
o: To port — she behaves like a right-handed prop
To port — the stern follows the side of the wash
Neither way — a fixed propeller has no prop walk
why: The wash comes out on the side opposite the kick: wash to port means the stern walks to starboard, as with a left-handed propeller.

fig.title: Taking over a charter boat
lines: Nobody knows which way she walks
Lines on, you go astern at 1500 rpm
The wash boils up along her port side

q: You reverse out of this pen into the fairway, turning the wheel to bring the stern round to port. Which part of the boat do you watch most closely?
a: The bow — going astern she pivots near the stern
o: The stern — going astern she pivots near the bow
The stern — the pivot point stays amidships
The keel — she pivots on it whichever way she goes
why: Going astern the pivot point moves aft, so the bow sweeps a wide arc and can hit the boat beside you as you turn.

fig.note: Bow-in pen · a yacht 1 m off each side

q: You are leaving this pontoon with the stream from ahead and boats close ahead and astern. How do you get the bow out?
a: Single up to a stern spring, let go forward; the stream pushes the bow out
o: Single up to a bow spring, let go aft; the stream pushes the stern out
Let go everything and motor out with the helm hard over
Single up to a stern line led aft and go slow astern
why: The stream from ahead holds her back on the stern spring and gets between bow and pontoon; once the bow is out, go ahead and slip.
ref: Leaving a berth — using the stream

fig.note: Starboard side to · wind light

q: You are leaving this bow-in berth astern, with the wind on the beam. How do you do it?
a: Slip the leeward lines, the windward ones last; go astern firmly
o: Slip the windward lines first, then go astern dead slow
Slip the leeward lines first, then go astern dead slow
Slip every line at once and let her drift out astern
why: The windward lines hold her off the yacht to leeward until the last moment; firm sternway gives the rudder grip before the bow blows off.
ref: Leaving a berth in a crosswind

fig.note: Wind E 4, on the starboard beam · finger to starboard

q: You are coming alongside this pontoon with the wind blowing you onto it. How do you make the approach?
a: Stop parallel, about a beam's width off, and let her blow in
o: Come in at 45° and turn parallel at the last moment
Come in parallel with way on and stop right alongside
Come in bow first and get the bow line on before the stern
why: With the wind onto the berth, stop level with it a little way off: she drifts in square, with fenders low and lines ready fore and aft.

fig.note: Berth: starboard side to

q: Your berth is on the leeward side of this pontoon, so she will blow off it as soon as she stops. What approach do you plan?
a: A steeper angle with more way; the midships line on first
o: A shallow angle, dead slow; the stern line on first
Stop parallel a beam's width off and let her drift in
A steeper angle, dead slow; the bow line on first
why: Blown off, she must be got in before she stops: a steeper angle with enough way, then the midships line holds her while you motor in on it.

fig.note: Berth: port side to · wind off the pontoon

q: You are picking up a mooring here under power, with the wind against the tide. Which way do you head for the final approach?
a: West, into the wind, as the moored yachts lie
o: East, into the stream — a buoy is always taken uptide
East, with the wind astern, to keep good steerage
North, across both, and stop beside the buoy
why: Approach the way the moored boats lie: here the F5 wind beats the weak stream, so she stops best heading west, into it.

fig.note: Wind against tide

q: Your bow crew has the buoy's pick-up line on the boat hook, but the bow is falling away fast and the hook is being dragged from her hands. What should she do?
a: Let go of the hook; you will come round again
o: Hold on and lean back to stop the boat
Jam the handle against the pulpit and hold on
Kneel down and hold on with both hands
why: A boat hook cannot hold a yacht: let it go, keep the crew aboard, and make another approach slower and closer.
ref: Picking up a mooring — the boat hook

fig.note: Pick-up hooked · the bow is falling away

q: You stop for lunch on this buoy and will sail off it later. How do you make fast?
a: A slip line through the ring, both ends cleated aboard
o: A bowline through the ring, its tail cleated aboard
A clove hitch round the ring, its tail cleated aboard
A round turn and two half hitches on the ring
why: A slip line is let go from the deck in seconds — one end freed and pulled back through — with no one reaching down to the buoy.

fig.note: Lunch stop, then you sail off

q: You are going stern-to in this lazy-line marina with the wind across the berth. Which line goes on first?
a: The windward stern line, then the lazy line to the bow
o: The leeward stern line, then the lazy line to the bow
The lazy line first, then both stern lines together
Both stern lines first, then the lazy line at leisure
why: The windward stern line stops her blowing down onto the next boat; then the lazy line, taken forward quickly, holds the bow up.

fig.note: Lazy-line marina · wind W 4 across the berth

q: You are ready to leave this berth. In what order do you let go?
a: Drop the lazy line, let it sink, slip the stern lines, go
o: Slip the stern lines, go ahead, then drop the lazy line
Drop the lazy line and go ahead hard as it sinks
Slip every line at once and motor straight out
why: The lazy line must be on the bottom before the propeller turns ahead; the stern lines hold her while it sinks.

fig.title: Leaving a lazy-line berth
lines: Stern lines and lazy line on
Engine running, crew at bow and stern

q: You are the inside boat of this raft and must leave first. How do you get out?
a: Out astern, down-tide; she swings in on a bow line to the quay
o: Out ahead, up-tide; she swings in on a stern line to the quay
Out ahead, up-tide, once she has let go and motored clear
Out astern, down-tide; she swings in on a stern line to the quay
why: Leave down-tide: the outer boat keeps her up-tide bow line, now led to the quay, and the stream swings her in behind you.

fig.note: You: inside, port side to the quay

q: You are towing the dinghy and are about to reverse into a Med berth. What do you do with it first?
a: Pull it alongside on a short painter, clear of the prop
o: Leave it astern on its long painter as it is
Pull it right up under the stern, against the transom
Lengthen the painter so it trails well clear
why: Going astern you run over your own painter; tie the dinghy short alongside, forward of the propeller, before you reverse.

q: You will sail onto anchor at X, among the other yachts. How do you make the final approach?
a: Under main alone, luff to stop, let go as she falls back
o: Under jib alone, run in downwind and let go at speed
Under full sail, let go at speed so the anchor bites
Under main alone, let go while she still has way on
why: The main alone lets her luff head to wind and stop; let go as she gathers sternway, so the chain lays out and the anchor sets.

fig.note: Wind N 3 · no stream · • yachts at anchor

q: You are lying to the stream on this mooring, with the wind from astern. How do you sail off?
a: Unroll the jib, slip, and sail clear; hoist the main later
o: Hoist the main, slip, and bear away clear
Hoist main and jib, slip, and sail off close-hauled
Hoist the main, slip, and let the stream carry you back
why: With the wind from astern the main cannot go up cleanly — it fills against the shrouds; the jib alone is set and furled at will.

fig.note: Lying head to the stream · moorings all round

q: The watch leader calls you below. When and how do you reef?
a: Now, from the cockpit, everyone clipped on, the main eased
o: At F6, when the reef is really needed
At dawn, when everyone can see what they are doing
Now, bearing away to a run to take the load off
why: Reef early at night: the work is slower in the dark, so do it before it is urgent — clipped on, main eased, lines led aft.

fig.title: 0200, watch of two
lines: Wind SW 5 and rising, F6 forecast
Slab reefing, lines led to the cockpit

q: You need to roll away half the genoa. How do you do it?
a: Ease the sheet under control while you pull in the furling line
o: Let the sheet fly, then winch in the furling line
Winch in the furling line with the sheet still hard on
Luff head to wind and let it flog while you furl
why: Some tension on the sheet rolls the sail tight and even; a flogging genoa rolls loose and chafes, and a sheet left hard on overloads the furler.

fig.note: F6 · furling genoa · the main already reefed

q: You have been running with a preventer for hours and must now gybe. What do you do first?
a: Free the preventer and sheet the main in to the centre
o: Gybe with the preventer on; it controls the boom
Free the preventer as the boom swings across
Ease the main right out, then put the helm over
why: A preventer left on stops the gybe and lays her over; free it, centre the boom, gybe, ease out, then re-rig it on the new side.

fig.note: Running for hours, preventer on · time to gybe

q: You are running with the boom out to starboard, and the wind has crept round to where the figure shows it. What do you do?
a: Turn a few degrees to port, to bring the wind to port
o: Turn a few degrees to starboard, to run deeper
Ease the main right out against the shroud
Hold on; the kicker will keep the boom out
why: Wind on the same side as the boom means you are by the lee and close to a gybe; turn away from the boom side until the wind is on the other quarter.

fig.note: Wind over the starboard quarter · boom to starboard

q: You plan to heave to here until it is light. Is there room?
a: No — about 4.8 M of drift; heave to further out
o: Yes — hove to, she lies almost stopped
Yes — about 1.2 M of drift leaves 2.8 M spare
Yes — about 3.6 M of drift leaves a margin
why: Hove to she still drifts: 4 h × 1.2 kn = 4.8 M, more than the 4 M to the shore. Heave to with room to spare.

fig.title: Waiting for daylight
lines: The lee shore is 4 M downwind

q: Your catamaran keeps stopping head to wind when you tack in this chop. What do you change?
a: Hold the jib aback until the bows are well through
o: Let the jib sheet fly as soon as the helm goes over
Put the helm over slowly so she loses less speed
Sheet the main hard in as you come through the wind
why: Light and with little keel, a cat loses way fast head to wind; the backed jib pushes the bows round onto the new tack.

fig.note: Catamaran · F4, short chop · she stalls tacking

q: She won't point, and you hold the tiller to leeward to stop her bearing away in the gusts. What do you do?
a: Roll away some genoa to bring the balance aft
o: Ease the mainsheet to take power out of the main
Move the crew forward to lift the stern
Sheet the genoa in harder to make her point
why: Lee helm means too much sail forward: with two reefs in the main, reduce the genoa until the helm is near neutral or a little weather.

fig.note: Two reefs in the main, full genoa · F5

q: A yacht with a failed engine asks you for a tow into harbour, 6 miles away. Which of your lines do you use as the towline?
a: The nylon anchor warp, for its stretch
o: The Dyneema spare halyard, for its strength
The polyester genoa sheets, joined together
The floating dinghy painter, for safety
why: Nylon stretches and absorbs the snatch of a tow; low-stretch line shock-loads the cleats, and a thin painter can part.

q: The tow has two hours still to run. What do you do about the towline?
a: Lengthen it, hang a weight in the middle, pad the fairlead
o: Shorten it so the line never goes slack
Speed up so the line stays tight all the time
Swap to a low-stretch line that won't snatch
why: A longer line with a weight in the middle sags and cushions each snatch; a chafe guard at the fairlead stops it wearing through.

fig.title: Towing, hour three of five
lines: 40 m of nylon out, moderate swell
Line jerks bar-tight every few waves

q: You will tow this yacht to harbour. What speed and ETA do you plan?
a: 5 kn, ETA 1524
o: 5 kn, ETA 1540
7 kn, ETA 1409
7 kn, ETA 1414
why: Tow well below her hull speed: 22 ÷ 5 = 4.4 h = 4 h 24 min, so 1100 + 4 h 24 min = 1524.

fig.title: A long tow
lines: Her hull speed is about 7 kn
You can tow at 5 or at 7 kn

q: You will tow this yacht with your boat. Where do you make the towline fast?
a: A bridle from both quarters, so the pull is central
o: One stern cleat, on the side the wind comes from
The backstay chainplate, in the middle of the stern
The pushpit rail, high enough to clear the rudder
why: A bridle across both quarters spreads the load and keeps the pull central, so you can still steer; a pushpit or backstay fitting is not built for it.

fig.note: You are towing · one towline

q: You have towed this yacht to the marina entrance. How do you take her the last 400 m?
a: Alongside, your stern aft of hers, lines and springs tight
o: Astern on a short towline, at dead slow speed
Alongside, bows level, with bow and stern lines only
Alongside, your bow ahead of hers, with one spring
why: An alongside tow steers like one boat: your rudder and prop aft of her stern, and tight springs to take the load ahead and astern.

fig.title: Into the marina
lines: Last 400 m through a tight marina
Calm; you are an 11 m yacht

q: You are holding your catamaran beam-on to the wind while you wait for a berth, and her bows keep blowing off. How do you bring them back up without moving ahead?
a: Leeward engine ahead, windward engine astern
o: Windward engine ahead, leeward engine astern
Both engines ahead, the rudders to windward
Leeward engine astern, windward one in neutral
why: The bows have less grip and blow off first; leeward ahead with windward astern turns her on the spot, bows towards the wind.

fig.note: Twin-engine catamaran · bows blowing off

q: Your catamaran is pinned to this pontoon, with boats close ahead and astern. How do you swing the stern out to leave astern?
a: Port engine ahead, starboard engine in neutral
o: Starboard engine ahead, port engine in neutral
Port engine astern, starboard engine in neutral
Both engines ahead, the rudders hard to port
why: On the bow spring the outboard engine's thrust, far from the spring, swings the stern out; then both astern to back away.

fig.note: Catamaran · wind W 5 · bow spring on

q: How do you tow the dinghy on this passage?
a: Outboard aboard, two painters, on the back of a wave
o: Outboard left on, one painter, close under the stern
Outboard left on, one painter, as long as it will go
Outboard aboard, one painter, right up to the transom
why: Lift the outboard aboard, add a second painter in case one parts, and set the length so she rides on the back of a following wave.

fig.title: Before a 12-mile passage
lines: Forecast: following wind F4, short sea
